analysis.one_liner: Lets federal regulators oversee and regulate credit default swaps and other swap agreements.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan Senate bill to lift the legal ban on regulating credit default swaps was referred to the Banking Committee and never received a vote, a markup, or a hearing.
analysis.plain_summary: Since 2000, federal law had explicitly barred financial regulators from regulating credit default swaps and other swap agreements — the contracts whose unregulated use helped cause the 2008 financial crisis and the AIG bailout. This bill repealed those prohibitions and authorized the SEC, the CFTC, and other financial regulators to oversee swaps, require disclosure, and write and enforce rules for them. It was introduced in May 2009 by Senator Carl Levin with Republican Senator Susan Collins as cosponsor and died in the Senate Banking Committee without any action.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers and anyone who depends on a stable financial system: the bill would have closed the regulatory gap that let giant, unregulated swap positions pile up and collapse in 2008, triggering bailouts paid for by taxpayers. Businesses like airlines and manufacturers that use swaps to hedge risks would also have gained clearer, safer markets.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the provisions of the Commodity Futures Modernization Act of 2000, the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act, and related laws that prohibited federal regulators from regulating credit default swaps and other swap agreements, whether traded on an exchange or privately over the counter.

Authorizes the SEC, the CFTC, and other federal financial regulators to exercise oversight over any swap agreement within their jurisdiction and to write, interpret, and enforce regulations, including disclosure, reporting, and recordkeeping requirements.
Assigns the SEC sole oversight over exchanges and clearing agencies and the CFTC sole oversight over trading facilities, and requires regulators to cooperate to keep rules consistent across agencies.

analysis.who_pays: Large banks and other dealers in the over-the-counter swap market, who had operated free of federal oversight since 2000 and would face disclosure, reporting, and capital rules. Hedging could also become somewhat more expensive for businesses that use swaps.

drawbacks.text: The bill gave oversight powers to seven-plus regulators with overlapping jurisdiction over the same contracts; its consultation requirement aimed at consistency, but fragmentation could have left gaps or conflicting rules. Congress ultimately addressed this differently in the Dodd-Frank law by assigning swaps to the CFTC and SEC along cleaner jurisdictional lines.
Regulating swaps adds compliance costs for dealers, and some of that cost passes to businesses and institutions that use swaps to hedge real-world risks like fuel prices and interest rates.
The bill authorized regulation but did not itself write any rules — its value depended entirely on what the regulators later did with the new authority.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill was a narrow, targeted fix: it did not dictate rules, it simply restored regulators' legal authority to write them. The main cost is compliance for dealers and slightly pricier hedging; the main benefit is reducing the chance of another unregulated derivatives collapse like the one behind the 2008 AIG bailout. As written, its main design weakness was relying on multiple regulators to coordinate rather than drawing clean jurisdictional lines, which the later Dodd-Frank law did instead.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which never took it up, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Carl Levin introduced the bill on May 4, 2009, with Senator Susan Collins as its cosponsor, making it a two-party effort from the start.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs on the day it was introduced.
No further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — was ever recorded before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Swap-dealing banks were better off in the near term, since the unregulated status quo continued while the bill sat untouched. The broader story: later that same Congress, the Dodd-Frank law enacted derivatives regulation through the normal committee process, so this bill's substance was largely covered even though the bill itself died.

for.name: Sen. Carl Levin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: Sen. Susan Collins
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only Republican to do so.

against.name: Sen. Christopher Dodd
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; instead authored the committee's own broader financial regulation bill, which became Dodd-Frank.

against.name: Major banks and swap dealers
against.what_they_did: Opposed derivatives regulation during the 2009-2010 debate; the industry spent heavily against it.

sides.party_line_note: A Democrat introduced it and a Republican cosponsored it — Senator Collins was 1 of 40 Senate Republicans on the bill — but with no votes ever held, no party split can be measured.

industries.note: Since 2000, federal law had prohibited regulators from touching their swap business; this bill repealed those prohibitions and subjected them to oversight, disclosure, and rulemaking. Their gain from the bill's death was the public's continued exposure to an unregulated market that helped cause the 2008 bailouts.

industries.industry: Clearing agencies, exchanges, and trading facilities
industries.note: The bill put swaps traded or cleared through exchanges under SEC and CFTC oversight, adding regulation for these venues, while the same rules would give cleared, exchange-traded swaps a defined legal home under a named regulator.

industries.industry: Corporate swap end users (airlines, manufacturers, municipalities)
industries.note: Their hedges would come under regulator oversight too, which could raise hedging costs slightly, but a supervised market reduces the chance that a counterparty like AIG fails and leaves them with worthless protection.
